cards.title: Introduction to React Testing
cards.content:
In modern web development, testing ensures your application works as expected. For React, the standard toolset is Jest (the test runner) and React Testing Library (RTL) (the UI testing library).

RTL encourages testing behavior rather than implementation details (like component state or internal methods).

import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import MyComponent from './MyComponent';

test('renders welcome message', () => {
  render(<MyComponent />);
  const linkElement = screen.getByText(/welcome/i);
  expect(linkElement).toBeInTheDocument();
});

pairs.value: Tests an isolated function, hook, or small stateless component.
Tests multiple components interacting together to achieve a workflow.
Tests the complete user flow inside a real headless or physical browser.

content.question: Which React Testing Library query type should be used when expecting an element to appear asynchronously after an API call finishes?

content.sentence: To mount a component into the virtual DOM for testing, we use the [blank1] utility. To simulate realistic user interactions (like keypresses), we should use the [blank2] library instead of fireEvent.

content.instruction: Order the steps of a React Testing Library test according to the industry standard AAA (Arrange, Act, Assert) workflow.

items.text: Arrange: Render the React component under test and set up mocks/props.
Act: Simulate user events like typing or clicking buttons.
Assert: Expect specific changes to have occurred in the DOM layout or mocks.

cards.title: Mocking APIs with MSW
cards.content:
When testing components that fetch data, we avoid hitting real APIs to keep tests fast and deterministic.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) is the recommended tool. It intercepts requests at the network level, allowing you to reuse the same mock handlers for development, testing, and debugging.

import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { rest } from 'msw';

const server = setupServer(
  rest.get('/api/user', (req, res, ctx) => {
    return res(ctx.json({ name: 'John Doe' }));
  })
);

content.question: Why is userEvent generally preferred over fireEvent in React Testing Library?

options.text: userEvent simulates the entire dispatch sequence of browser events (hover, focus, click), whereas fireEvent only dispatches single targeted DOM events.
